title: Planar graphs from local neighborhoods
formal: For every real \(\varepsilon>0\), does there exist a positive integer \(D=D(\varepsilon)\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every pair of finite simple planar graphs \(G,H\) on \(n\) vertices, equality of their multisets of rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhoods implies \[\min_{\phi:V(G)\cong V(H)}\left|\phi(E(G))\mathbin{\triangle}E(H)\right|\le\varepsilon n?\] The minimum is over all vertex bijections, and \(\triangle\) denotes symmetric difference of edge sets. There is no maximum-degree bound; the radius may depend only on \(\varepsilon\).
why: This asks whether local structure determines approximate global structure throughout the planar family, even around vertices of very high degree. It isolates a structural obstruction behind extending sparse-graph testing beyond bounded-degree and outerplanar settings.

sentences: The question compares two planar graphs through the rooted neighborhoods around all their vertices.
It asks whether a radius depending only on the allowed error makes identical neighborhood multisets imply closeness under edge edits and vertex relabeling.
No maximum-degree bound is imposed, so even a small-radius neighborhood may be large.
The source proves the analogous result for outerplanar graphs, while bounded-degree planar theorems allow the radius to depend on the degree bound.
This specific structural question replaces the original broad classification target by an explicitly selected yes/no assertion.

definitions:
A finite simple undirected graph is a finite vertex set \(V\) and a set \(E\) of unordered pairs of distinct vertices. Thus loops and multiple edges are excluded. A planar graph admits a drawing in the plane with distinct points for vertices and curves for edges whose interiors neither intersect one another nor meet a vertex. A drawing is not part of the data, and it is not used to compare neighborhoods. Graphs need not be connected. Their order is \(n=|V|\), and the two graphs in the question have the same order.

The graph distance \(\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path from \(u\) to \(v\), with distance infinity when no path exists. The rooted radius-\(D\) neighborhood \(B_G(v,D)\) is the subgraph induced by \(\{u\in V(G):\operatorname{dist}_G(u,v)\le D\}\), together with the distinguished root \(v\). An induced subgraph retains every edge whose two endpoints belong to that set. Rooted graphs are isomorphic when a bijection of their vertices preserves edges and sends one root to the other. Vertex labels, the planar drawing, any ordering of neighbors, and edges leaving the neighborhood are not part of its rooted isomorphism type.

The multiset of radius-\(D\) neighborhoods records each rooted isomorphism type with its multiplicity among the \(n\) possible roots. Equality means that, for every finite rooted graph \(F\), the number of vertices \(v\) for which \(B_G(v,D)\) is isomorphic to \(F\) equals the corresponding number in \(H\). Thus multiplicities matter. Although corresponding roots can be paired, their individual neighborhood isomorphisms need not agree on overlapping vertices. In particular, such a pairing is not already a global graph isomorphism. Even a radius-one neighborhood may contain arbitrarily many vertices, because degrees are unrestricted.

For a vertex bijection \(\phi:V(G)\to V(H)\), define \(\phi(E(G))=\{\{\phi(u),\phi(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E(G)\}\). The symmetric difference consists of edges in exactly one of its two arguments. Its cardinality counts edge deletions plus edge additions, each at unit cost, after a free relabeling of vertices. Taking the minimum over bijections gives the edit distance to isomorphism. There are no vertex edits or isolated-vertex padding in this equal-order question. Intermediate graphs during edge editing are not required to be planar. The permitted number of edits is at most \(\varepsilon n\), normalized by vertex count rather than by the number of possible edges or by a degree bound. For \(n=1\) the conclusion is automatic. No algorithm for finding the bijection, a computable bound on \(D\), or property-testing oracle is requested; this is a structural existence statement.

source_formulation.text: Do identical sufficiently large rooted local-neighborhood multisets force two planar graphs of the same order to be close to isomorphic under edge edits?

context_blocks.text: The broad imported question asked for a classification of graph properties testable with sublinear query complexity. This card now adopts the separate, concrete planar local-neighborhood question from the same source. The change of scope was explicitly selected on 16 September 2026; it does not claim to complete the original general classification programme.

The structural issue is whether sufficiently large local views determine a sparse planar graph up to a small linear number of edge edits. The neighborhoods carry no consistent global labels. Matching their multiplicities therefore supplies statistical local information, not a ready-made global correspondence.

For planar graphs with a fixed maximum degree, earlier local-to-global results provide a radius depending on both the error tolerance and that degree bound. The selected question asks whether the degree dependence can be removed completely. Planarity bounds average degree, but permits individual degrees growing with the graph order.

Babu, Khoury and Newman prove the required local-view implication for outerplanar graphs, with no maximum-degree bound. Outerplanar means that the graph has a plane drawing with every vertex incident to the exterior face. Their Theorem 4.4 states the same qualitative radius-versus-edge-distance conclusion for that subclass.

The source extends its methods to graphs with a fixed number of edge-removal outer layers. It distinguishes this from removing exterior vertices layer by layer, and explicitly retains the ordinary 2-outerplanar case as open at publication. Those positive results therefore must not be read as covering every planar graph.

The paper also obtains polylogarithmic-query property testers for its unbounded-degree subclasses, using ordered-neighbor and degree access. These algorithmic results explain the motivation for the structural question, but the selected target itself asks only for the stated finite-graph implication.

Basu, Kumar and Seshadhri sharpen the dependence on proximity for testing properties of bounded-degree planar graphs and show matching exponential behavior for isomorphism testing. Their results retain a maximum-degree bound and therefore do not settle the unbounded-degree local-view question.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed universal statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation: there exists a fixed \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that for every positive integer \(D\), there are some \(n\ge1\) and simple planar \(n\)-vertex graphs \(G,H\) with identical radius-\(D\) neighborhood multisets but edit distance strictly greater than \(\varepsilon_0 n\). The counterexample graphs and their orders may depend on \(D\); the same positive \(\varepsilon_0\) must work throughout. A proof restricted to bounded maximum degree or to outerplanar graphs does not establish the assertion for all planar graphs. Equality of the set of neighborhood types without multiplicities is a different hypothesis. A radius growing with \(n\) or maximum degree is insufficient. This is an exact yes/no implication, not a numerical approximation problem.
